name: Wails
summary: A Go desktop application framework that embeds web frontend assets in a native window, exposes Go methods through generated JavaScript and TypeScript bindings, and provides a runtime event and window-control bridge.

features.name: Go and webview application shell
features.description: A Wails application is a Go program whose application configuration creates a native window and loads frontend assets into a webkit-based view. The official architecture documentation describes the Go runtime and frontend as cooperating parts of one desktop process.
benefits: Reuses web UI tooling inside a native desktop shell
Keeps application lifecycle and window control in Go
costs: Webview engine behavior varies by operating system
Native and browser execution models must be coordinated

features.name: Generated Go-to-JavaScript bindings
features.description: The Bind option exposes public methods on Go struct instances; Wails generates JavaScript wrappers, TypeScript declarations, and models for bound data so the frontend can call Go methods asynchronously.
benefits: Reduces handwritten serialization and bridge code
Provides typed frontend declarations for bound methods and models
costs: Generated API shape follows exported Go methods and JSON tags
Calls cross an asynchronous process/runtime boundary

features.name: Runtime event and window bridge
features.description: The Wails runtime exposes frontend-callable operations for application events and native window behavior. This creates an explicit bridge between web code and the Go/native shell rather than treating the frontend as a standalone browser page.
benefits: Allows frontend code to request native capabilities
Supports event-based coordination between frontend and application
costs: Event names, payloads, and lifecycle timing are bridge contracts

mathematical_views.question: How do exported Go methods and data models map to generated frontend calls and results across the webview boundary?
assumptions: Generated wrappers represent typed request and response edges
Asynchronous completion and errors are modeled as transitions

mathematical_views.question: How do Go startup and shutdown callbacks, frontend readiness, window events, and runtime calls transition the desktop application?
assumptions: Go and frontend have distinct but coordinated lifecycle states
The webview loads assets before frontend readiness
The model abstracts OS-specific webview details

benefits: Web UI with native desktop packaging
costs: Webview and OS differences remain operational concerns
Generated contracts and async errors constrain integration
Bridge lifecycle and payload contracts need coordination
